claims.source: Consistently, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1/A2 (before CK-666 addition) and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A3/A4 (after CK-666 addition) together show that CK-666 addition leads not only to a reduction in the size of the dSMAC (magenta brackets), but also to an increase in arc content in the pSMAC (blue brackets).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Following CK-666 treatment, there is a significant shift away from dSMAC F-actin and toward pSMAC F-actin.
claims.source: These changes were supported by measuring the percentage of total synaptic F-actin content residing within each SMAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), which revealed a significant shift away from dSMAC F-actin and toward pSMAC F-actin following CK-666 treatment.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The shift in F-actin distribution following CK-666 treatment was reflected in measurements of total pSMAC F-actin content, the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC F-actin content, and the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC area.
claims.source: This shift was also reflected in measurements of total pSMAC F-actin content (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC F-actin content (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), and the ratio of pSMAC to cSMAC area (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-E.

claims.claim: Linear actin filaments generated by the formin mDia1 at the outer edge of the synapse give rise to the pSMAC actin arc network.
claims.source: Taken together, these data argue strongly that linear actin filaments generated by the formin mDia1 at the outer edge of the synapse give rise to the pSMAC actin arc network.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data on formin inhibition, mDia1 knockdown, and Arp2/3 inhibition.

claims.claim: Formin-derived linear actin filaments are commonly organized into well-defined structures such as stress fibers, transverse arcs, and the contractile ring in dividing cells by bipolar filaments of myosin 2.
claims.source: Formin-derived linear actin filaments are commonly organized into well-defined structures such as stress fibers, transverse arcs, and the contractile ring in dividing cells by bipolar filaments of the actin-based motor protein myosin 2 (Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2009; Sellers, 2000; Shutova and Svitkina, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by three citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: M2A is the only myosin 2 isoform expressed in B cells.
claims.source: To define the localization and dynamics of myosin 2 at the B-cell IS, we used primary B cells isolated from a mouse in which GFP had been knocked into the N- terminus of the myosin 2A heavy chain gene Myh9 (referred to herein as M2A) (Zhang et al., 2012) as M2A is the only myosin 2 isoform expressed in B cells (ImmGen Database).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a fact based on the ImmGen Database.

claims.claim: M2A co-localizes dramatically with the actin arcs in the pSMAC.
claims.source: Individual video frames of these cells following transfection with Td-Tomato-F-Tractin and attachment to coverslips coated with anti-IgM and ICAM-1 revealed a dramatic co-localization between M2A and the actin arcs in the pSMAC (Figure 3A1–A3, Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3A1-A3 and Video 6.

claims.claim: The myosin signals align with actin arcs in a periodic fashion that resembles other myosin 2-rich, linear actin structures like stress fibers and the contractile ring.
claims.source: Magnified TIRF-SIM images show that the myosin signals align with actin arcs in a periodic fashion (Figure 3A4) that resembles other myosin 2-rich, linear actin structures like stress fibers and the contractile ring (Beach et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3A4, with comparison to prior work cited.

claims.claim: The myosin signals exhibit the SIM signature for M2A bipolar filaments when M2A is GFP-labeled at its N-terminus, which is a pair of GFP puncta spaced ~300 nm apart.
claims.source: Moreover, these myosin signals exhibit the SIM signature for M2A bipolar filaments when M2A is GFP-labeled at its N-terminus (Beach et al., 2017), which is a pair of GFP puncta spaced ~300 nm apart (Figure 3A5; 304 ± 32 nm; n = 230 filaments from 12 cells).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3A5 and quantification, with comparison to prior work cited.

claims.claim: The presence of M2A filaments in the medial portion of the synapse was evident in primary B cells isolated from a mouse in which mCherry had been knocked into the N-terminus of M2A.
claims.source: The presence of M2A filaments in the medial portion of the synapse was also evident in primary B cells isolated from a mouse in which mCherry had been knocked into the N-terminus of M2A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), primary B cells that we genome-edited using CRISPR to place GFP at the N-terminus of M2A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and A20 B cells that we genome edited using CRISPR to place mScarleti at the N-terminus of M2A and then transfected with GFP-F-Tractin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C1–C3, Video 5B).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C and Video 5B.

claims.claim: 3D-SIM images of fixed and stained A20 B cells showed that endogenous M2A co-localizes with the actin arcs.
claims.source: Finally, 3D-SIM images of A20 B cells that were fixed and stained for M2A and F-actin showed that endogenous M2A also co-localizes with the actin arcs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D1–D3; note that the signature for M2A filaments using this antibody, which recognizes the C-terminus of M2A, is a single fluorescent punctum that corresponds to the center of an individual M2A filament) (Beach et al., 2014; Beach and Hammer, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D1-D3, with explanation supported by citations.

claims.claim: The actin arc network in primary B cells receiving ICAM-1 co-stimulation is an actomyosin arc network.
claims.source: Together, these results show that the actin arc network in primary B cells receiving ICAM-1 co-stimulation is in fact an actomyosin arc network.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-localization data.

claims.claim: Bipolar filaments of M2A begin to appear near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary in association with the linear actin filaments/bundles exiting the dSMAC.
claims.source: Individual video frames (Figure 3B1–B6), as well as the corresponding video (Video 7), show that bipolar filaments of M2A begin to appear near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary in association with the linear actin filaments/bundles exiting the dSMAC (white, yellow, and fuchsia arrowheads mark such myosin filaments at time 0 s in Figure 3B1).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B1-B6 and Video 7.

claims.claim: As time progresses, M2A filaments move centripetally and undergo expansion into filament clusters.
claims.source: As time progresses, these filaments move centripetally and undergo expansion into filament clusters (Figure 3B1–B6; see also Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B1-B6 and Video 7.

claims.claim: The expansion of M2A filaments into clusters is presumably driven by the same sequential amplification pathway described previously for M2A filament assembly in fibroblasts.
claims.source: This expansion, in which individual myosin filaments expand into a small cluster of filaments, is presumably driven by the same sequential amplification pathway described previously for M2A filament assembly in fibroblasts (Beach et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to prior work cited.

claims.claim: The myosin filaments in M2A clusters begin to align with the arcs forming at the outer edge of the pSMAC, which then merge with the larger actomyosin arc network in the pSMAC.
claims.source: Finally, the myosin filaments in these clusters begin to align with the arcs forming at the outer edge of the pSMAC, which then merge with the larger actomyosin arc network in the pSMAC (Figure 3B1–B6).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B1-B6.

claims.claim: New myosin filaments keep appearing near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary to repeat the process of assembly and organization.
claims.source: As all this is happening, new myosin filaments keep appearing near the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary to repeat the process (Figure 3B2–B6; follow the blue, green, and purple arrowheads).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3B2-B6.

claims.claim: Primary GFP-M2A knockin B cells receiving both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 stimulation exhibited a greater amount of synaptic M2A than B cells receiving only anti-IgM stimulation.
claims.source: Consistently, primary GFP-M2A knockin B cells receiving both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 stimulation exhibited a greater amount of synaptic M2A than B cells receiving only anti-IgM stimulation (Figure 3C–E).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C-E.

claims.claim: The difference in synaptic M2A between cells receiving anti-IgM alone versus anti-IgM + ICAM-1 remained significant even after normalizing for cell-spread area.
claims.source: Of note, this difference remained significant even after normalizing the M2A fluorescence for a small difference in the average cell-spread area under these two conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G1–G2).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G1-G2.

claims.claim: Cells treated with 25 μM pnBB displayed highly disorganized, mesh-like actin arrays in their pSMAC, while control DMSO-treated cells exhibited concentric actin arcs.
claims.source: While control, DMSO-treated cells exhibited concentric actin arcs in their pSMAC as expected (Figure 3F), cells treated with 25 μM pnBB displayed highly disorganized, mesh-like actin arrays in their pSMAC (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: Anisotropy measurements revealed a dramatic shift towards more disorganized pSMAC actin when B cells are treated with pnBB.
claims.source: Consistently, anisotropy measurements made using FibrilTool revealed a dramatic shift towards more disorganized pSMAC actin when B cells are treated with pnBB (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: M2A contractility is required for the concentric organization of the pSMAC actin arcs.
claims.source: Together, these results demonstrate that M2A contractility is indeed required for the concentric organization of the pSMAC actin arcs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pnBB treatment experiments.

claims.claim: B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM and ICAM-1 generated significantly more traction force than B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM alone.
claims.source: As expected (Wang, 2018; Kumari et al., 2019), B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM and ICAM-1 generated significantly more traction force than B cells engaged with substrate coated with anti-IgM alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A1, A2, B1, B2, and D).
claims.evidence: This is based on traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, with comparison to prior work cited.

claims.claim: ICAM-1-dependent traction forces were completely abrogated by pretreating the cells with pnBB.
claims.source: Importantly, ICAM-1-dependent traction forces were completely abrogated by pretreating the cells with pnBB (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C1, C2, and D), indicating that the generation of integrin-dependent traction forces requires M2A contractility.
claims.evidence: This is based on traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: The generation of integrin-dependent traction forces requires M2A contractility.
claims.source: Importantly, ICAM-1-dependent traction forces were completely abrogated by pretreating the cells with pnBB (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C1, C2, and D), indicating that the generation of integrin-dependent traction forces requires M2A contractility.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pnBB treatment experiments on traction forces.

claims.claim: The requirement for M2A contractility in traction force generation likely reflects pulling forces exerted by M2A on the substrate through LFA-1:ICAM-1 pairs, combined with the increase in M2A content at the synapse caused by ligating LFA-1 with ICAM-1, and the contribution that M2A-dependent pulling forces make in keeping LFA-1 in its open, active conformation.
claims.source: This requirement likely reflects pulling forces exerted by M2A on the substrate through LFA-1:ICAM-1 pairs, combined with the increase in M2A content at the synapse caused by ligating LFA-1 with ICAM-1, and the contribution that M2A-dependent pulling forces make in keeping LFA-1 in its open, active conformation (Gardel et al., 2010; Case and Waterman, 2015; Comrie and Burkhardt, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism supported by three citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Integrin clusters are known to accumulate in the pSMAC portion of the B-cell IS.
claims.source: These results, together with the fact that integrin clusters are known to accumulate in the pSMAC portion of the B-cell IS (Carrasco et al., 2004; Carrasco and Batista, 2006b), suggest a feed-forward relationship where integrin ligation promotes the formation of pSMAC actomyosin arcs, and the contractile forces exerted by these actomyosin arcs promote further integrin activation and robust adhesion in the pSMAC.
claims.evidence: This is stated as known fact supported by two citations.

claims.claim: There is a feed-forward relationship where integrin ligation promotes the formation of pSMAC actomyosin arcs, and the contractile forces exerted by these actomyosin arcs promote further integrin activation and robust adhesion in the pSMAC.
claims.source: These results, together with the fact that integrin clusters are known to accumulate in the pSMAC portion of the B-cell IS (Carrasco et al., 2004; Carrasco and Batista, 2006b), suggest a feed-forward relationship where integrin ligation promotes the formation of pSMAC actomyosin arcs, and the contractile forces exerted by these actomyosin arcs promote further integrin activation and robust adhesion in the pSMAC.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data and prior knowledge.

claims.claim: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network flows centripetally at 1.07 ± 0.07 µm/min in primary B cells.
claims.source: Kymograph analyses of actin flow across synapses made by primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin showed that their pSMAC actomyosin arc network indeed flows centripetally at 1.07 ± 0.07 µm/min, or about one-third the rate of centripetal actin flow in the dSMAC (2.89 ± 0.18 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
claims.evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1-A3.

claims.claim: The dSMAC exhibits centripetal actin flow at 2.89 ± 0.18 µm/min in primary B cells.
claims.source: Kymograph analyses of actin flow across synapses made by primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin showed that their pSMAC actomyosin arc network indeed flows centripetally at 1.07 ± 0.07 µm/min, or about one-third the rate of centripetal actin flow in the dSMAC (2.89 ± 0.18 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
claims.evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1-A3.

claims.claim: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network flows centripetally at 0.97 ± 0.13 µm/min in A20 B cells.
claims.source: Similar results were obtained for A20 B cells (pSMAC rate: 0.97 ± 0.13 µm/min; dSMAC rate: 3.16 ± 0.35 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1–B3).
claims.evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1-B3.

claims.claim: The dSMAC exhibits centripetal actin flow at 3.16 ± 0.35 µm/min in A20 B cells.
claims.source: Similar results were obtained for A20 B cells (pSMAC rate: 0.97 ± 0.13 µm/min; dSMAC rate: 3.16 ± 0.35 µm/min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1–B3).
claims.evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B1-B3.

claims.claim: The actomyosin arcs could contribute along with the branched actin network in the dSMAC to the inward transport of BCR:antigen clusters.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that the actomyosin arcs could contribute along with the branched actin network in the dSMAC to the inward transport of BCR:antigen clusters.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the centripetal flow data.

claims.claim: Primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin readily formed actin arcs when PLBs contained both anti-IgM and ICAM-1, but not when they contained anti-IgM alone.
claims.source: As expected, primary B cells expressing GFP-F-Tractin readily formed actin arcs when PLBs contained both anti-IgM and ICAM-1 (Video 8A), but not when they contained anti-IgM alone (Video 8B).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Video 8A and 8B.

claims.claim: Primary B cells engaged with PLBs containing fluorescent anti-IgM and unlabeled ICAM-1 yielded mature synapses in which concentric actin arcs surrounded antigen accumulated in the cSMAC.
claims.source: Also as expected, primary B cells engaged with PLBs containing fluorescent anti-IgM (magenta) and unlabeled ICAM-1 yielded mature synapses in which concentric actin arcs surrounded antigen accumulated in the cSMAC (Figure 4A1–A3, white arrows).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 4A1-A3.

claims.claim: Single-antigen microclusters moved inward at 2.36 ± 1.1 µm/min across the dSMAC and 1.03 ± 0.3 µm/min across the pSMAC.
claims.source: Tracking of single-antigen microclusters showed that they moved inward at 2.36 ± 1.1 µm/min and 1.03 ± 0.3 µm/min across the dSMAC (magenta tracks) and pSMAC (green tracks), respectively (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on tracking data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: The rates of antigen microcluster movement are very similar to the rates of centripetal actin flow across the dSMAC and pSMAC.
claims.source: Importantly, these rates are very similar to the rates of centripetal actin flow across the dSMAC and pSMAC, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between the antigen tracking data and the actin flow data.

claims.claim: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network works together with the dSMAC branched actin network to drive antigen centralization.
claims.source: Together, these observations argue that the pSMAC actomyosin arc network works together with the dSMAC branched actin network to drive antigen centralization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similarity in rates between actin flow and antigen movement.

claims.claim: Individual actin arcs move individual BCR:antigen microclusters inward via a sweeping mechanism that likely depends on frictional coupling between the actin arc and microcluster.
claims.source: Together, these results argue that individual actin arcs move individual BCR:antigen microclusters inward via a sweeping mechanism that likely depends on frictional coupling between the actin arc and microcluster (Yu et al., 2010; Ditlev et al., 2019; Smoligovets et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from high-magnification imaging data, with mechanism supported by three citations.

claims.claim: The overall incidence of arcs slipping past microclusters must be fairly small as the rate of inward antigen transport across the pSMAC is not significantly slower than the rate of inward actin arc flow across the pSMAC.
claims.source: While arcs can slip past microclusters, the overall incidence of such slippage must be fairly small as the rate of inward antigen transport across the pSMAC (Figure 4C) is not significantly slower than the rate of inward actin arc flow across the pSMAC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A3).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the rates of antigen movement and actin flow.

claims.claim: B cells engaged with membrane-bound antigen at low density fail to centralize antigen unless their integrin LFA-1 is also engaged with ICAM-1 in the target membrane.
claims.source: B cells engaged with membrane-bound antigen at low density fail to centralize antigen unless their integrin LFA-1 is also engaged with ICAM-1 in the target membrane (Carrasco et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a known finding supported by citation to Carrasco et al., 2004.

claims.claim: B cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation over 10 min without the need for ICAM-1 when the PLB was loaded with anti-IgM at 2 µg/ml (high-density antigen).
claims.source: B cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation over 10 min without the need for ICAM-1 when the PLB was loaded using a solution containing anti-IgM at a concentration of 2 µg/ml (hereafter referred to as 'high-density antigen') (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A1–A3).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A1-A3.

claims.claim: B cells formed antigen microclusters across their synaptic interface but failed to centralize them over 10 min when the PLB was loaded with anti-IgM at 0.15 µg/ml (low or limiting density antigen).
claims.source: By contrast, B cells formed antigen microclusters across their synaptic interface but failed to centralize them over 10 min when the PLB was loaded using a solution containing anti-IgM at a concentration 0.15 µg/ml (hereafter referred to as 'low or limiting density antigen') (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B1–B3).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B1-B3.

claims.claim: When unlabeled ICAM-1 was included in low-density antigen bilayers, B cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation.
claims.source: Importantly, when unlabeled ICAM-1 was included in these low-density antigen bilayers, B cells now exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C1–C3).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C1-C3.

claims.claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 on antigen centralization was supported by scoring antigen distribution as centralized, partially centralized or noncentralized.
claims.source: This co-stimulatory effect was supported by scoring antigen distribution as centralized, partially centralized or noncentralized (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D1–D3 and E).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claims.claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 was supported by scoring the percent of total synaptic antigen present within the cSMAC.
claims.source: It was also supported by scoring the percent of total synaptic antigen present within the cSMAC, which was defined by a circular area encompassing 20% of the entire synaptic interface and centered around the center of mass of the fluorescent antigen-containing pixels within the interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The co-stimulatory effect of ICAM-1 was supported by measuring the size of antigen clusters as a function of their distance from the center of the cSMAC.
claims.source: Finally, it was supported by measuring the size of antigen clusters as a function of their distance from the center of the cSMAC (defined as above) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: B cells engaged with PLBs containing antigen at the limiting density and no ICAM-1 exhibited small antigen clusters (~0.3 µm2) located roughly evenly across the synaptic interface.
claims.source: Specifically, B cells engaged with PLBs containing antigen at the limiting density and no ICAM-1 exhibited small antigen clusters (~0.3 µm2) located roughly evenly across the synaptic interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, black trace), while B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 in addition to antigen at the limiting density exhibited large antigen clusters (up to 3 µm2), the largest of which were located at the center of the cSMAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, green trace).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 in addition to antigen at the limiting density exhibited large antigen clusters (up to 3 µm2), the largest of which were located at the center of the cSMAC.
claims.source: Specifically, B cells engaged with PLBs containing antigen at the limiting density and no ICAM-1 exhibited small antigen clusters (~0.3 µm2) located roughly evenly across the synaptic interface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, black trace), while B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 in addition to antigen at the limiting density exhibited large antigen clusters (up to 3 µm2), the largest of which were located at the center of the cSMAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, green trace).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was greater for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM + ICAM-1 than for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM alone.
claims.source: Of note, the total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was also greater for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM + ICAM-1 than for cells engaged with low-density anti-IgM alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: DMSO-treated cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation when engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and anti-IgM at the limiting density.
claims.source: While DMSO-treated cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation (Figure 5A1–A3), pnBB-treated cells failed to centralize antigen/create a cSMAC (Figure 5B1–B3).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5A1-A3.

claims.claim: pnBB-treated cells failed to centralize antigen/create a cSMAC when engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and anti-IgM at the limiting density.
claims.source: While DMSO-treated cells exhibited robust antigen centralization/cSMAC formation (Figure 5A1–A3), pnBB-treated cells failed to centralize antigen/create a cSMAC (Figure 5B1–B3).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5B1-B3.

claims.claim: The actin arcs that surround centralized antigen in DMSO-treated cells were absent in pnBB-treated cells.
claims.source: Consistently, the actin arcs that surround centralized antigen in DMSO-treated cells (Figure 5C1–C3, white arrows) were absent in pnBB-treated cells (Figure 5D1–D3).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 5C1-C3 and 5D1-D3.

claims.claim: Myosin inhibition abrogates the integrin co-stimulatory effect on antigen centralization.
claims.source: The fact that myosin inhibition abrogates the integrin co-stimulatory effect was further supported by scoring antigen distribution in control and pnBB-treated cells as centralized, partially centralized, or noncentralized (Figure 5E), byscoring the percent of total synaptic antigen present within the cSMAC (Figure 5F), and bymeasuring the size of antigen clusters as a function of their distance from the center of the cSMAC (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5E-G.

claims.claim: The total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was greater for cells treated with DMSO than for cells treated with pnBB.
claims.source: Of note, the total amount of antigen present at the synaptic interface was also greater for cells treated with DMSO than for cells treated with pnBB (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The ability of integrin ligation to promote antigen centralization and cSMAC formation when antigen is limiting requires myosin contractility.
claims.source: Together, these results show that the ability of integrin ligation to promote antigen centralization and cSMAC formation when antigen is limiting requires myosin contractility.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pnBB treatment experiments under limiting antigen conditions.

claims.claim: The contractile actomyosin arc network created downstream of integrin ligation plays an important role in the mechanism by which LFA-1 co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation.
claims.source: This in turn argues that the contractile actomyosin arc network created downstream of integrin ligation plays an important role in the mechanism by which LFA-1 co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data on myosin's role in integrin-dependent IS formation.

claims.claim: DMSO-treated primary B cells engaged with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and limiting antigen exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD79a and anti-IgM concentrated in the cSMAC.
claims.source: Consistent with results above and with the known properties of CD79a, DMSO-treated primary B cells engaged for 10 min with PLBs containing ICAM-1 and limiting antigen and then fixed/stained for P-CD79a exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD79a and anti-IgM concentrated in the cSMAC (Figure 6A1–A4).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6A1-A4.

claims.claim: pnBB-treated B cells failed to form a clear cSMAC, resulting in CD79a and anti-IgM spread across the synapse.
claims.source: Also as expected, pnBB-treated B cells failed to form a clear cSMAC, resulting in CD79a and anti-IgM spread across the synapse (Figure 6B1–B4).
claims.evidence: This is based on imaging data shown in Figure 6B1-B4.

claims.claim: pnBB-treated cells exhibited a significant reduction relative to control cells in synaptic P-CD79a content.
claims.source: Importantly, quantitation showed that pnBB-treated cells also exhibited a significant reduction relative to control cells in synaptic P-CD79a content (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The defect in synaptic P-CD79a content was also seen after only 5 min on PLBs.
claims.source: This defect was also seen after only 5 min on PLBs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and the defects at both time points were not due to differences between BB-treated cells and control cells in synaptic CD79a content (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The defects in P-CD79a at 5 and 10 min were not due to differences between BB-treated cells and control cells in synaptic CD79a content.
claims.source: This defect was also seen after only 5 min on PLBs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and the defects at both time points were not due to differences between BB-treated cells and control cells in synaptic CD79a content (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: DMSO-treated primary B cells exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD19 enriched at the outer edge of the IgM concentrated in the cSMAC.
claims.source: DMSO-treated primary B cells engaged with PLBs as above exhibited robust cSMAC formation, with P-CD19 enriched at the outer edge of the IgM concentrated in the cSMAC (Figure 6D1–D4).

results.result: B-cell activation and immune synapse (IS) formation with membrane-bound antigens are actin-dependent processes that scale with antigen signal strength. IS formation involves a branched actin network in the dSMAC that drives cell spreading and centripetal flow, leading to antigen centralization required for robust BCR signaling and antigen internalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C14-C22 establish the foundational knowledge about B-cell IS formation being actin-dependent and involving centripetal actin flow. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to prior literature and represent established knowledge in the field that provides context for the current study.

results.result: LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions serve as co-stimulatory signals that promote B-cell activation and IS formation when antigen is limiting or weak. Prior work showed that ICAM-1 co-stimulation is increasingly required as antigen density decreases, with the effect being most dramatic for weaker antigens and dependent on LFA-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C31, and C139 summarize prior work from Carrasco et al., 2004 establishing the co-stimulatory role of LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions. These claims are well-supported by citations and provide the foundation for investigating the mechanism of integrin co-stimulation in the current study.

results.result: LFA-1:ICAM-1 interactions promote the formation of a highly organized actomyosin arc network in the pSMAC that dominates the B-cell IS. Super-resolution imaging revealed that B cells stimulated with anti-IgM + ICAM-1 exhibit dense, persistent concentric actin arcs in the pSMAC, while cells stimulated with anti-IgM alone show sparse, transient arcs and disorganized actin. The pSMAC comprises the major actin network at the IS when ICAM-1 is present.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C34-C41 present the primary discovery that ICAM-1 co-stimulation induces organized actomyosin arcs in the pSMAC. The claims are strongly supported by super-resolution imaging data (Figures 1, Videos 1-2) and quantitative analysis showing increased arc presence (~30% to ~70%), increased organization (anisotropy measurements), and dominance of the pSMAC network. The use of two imaging modalities (Airyscan and TIRF-SIM) strengthens the findings.

results.result: The pSMAC actin arcs are generated by linear actin filaments nucleated at the plasma membrane by the formin mDia1. Imaging showed continuity between linear filaments at surface spikes and pSMAC arcs. Pan-formin inhibition (SMIFH2) eliminated arcs, and mDia1 knockdown using three different miRNAs significantly reduced arc formation, while non-targeting miRNAs had no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C53 and C57 establish that mDia1 creates the pSMAC arcs. The evidence is strong: (1) imaging shows structural continuity (Figure 2A-C, Video 3), (2) SMIFH2 treatment eliminates arcs (Figure 2D-E), (3) three independent mDia1 miRNAs reduce arcs (Figure 2F-H), and (4) two non-targeting controls show no effect (Figure 2—supplement 1C-D). The use of multiple miRNAs and controls strengthens the specificity of the knockdown effect.

results.result: Inhibiting the Arp2/3 complex with CK-666 reduces the dSMAC and increases arc content in the pSMAC, consistent with competition between Arp2/3 and formins for actin monomers. This supports the conclusion that arcs are formin-generated.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 provide additional evidence for formin-dependent arc formation through Arp2/3 inhibition experiments. The data (Figure 2—supplement 2) show the expected reciprocal relationship between branched and linear actin networks, supporting the formin mechanism. This is consistent with known competition between nucleators for actin monomers.

results.result: Myosin 2A (M2A), the only myosin 2 isoform in B cells, co-localizes dramatically with pSMAC actin arcs in a periodic pattern characteristic of bipolar myosin filaments. M2A filaments exhibit the expected ~300 nm spacing between GFP puncta when labeled at the N-terminus. This co-localization was confirmed using multiple approaches including knockin mice, CRISPR-edited cells, and immunostaining.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 establish M2A organization of the arcs. The evidence is comprehensive: (1) dramatic co-localization in GFP-M2A knockin cells (Figure 3A, Video 6), (2) characteristic bipolar filament signature with ~300 nm spacing (Figure 3A5), (3) confirmation in mCherry-M2A knockin mice (Figure 3—supplement 1A), (4) CRISPR-edited cells (Figure 3—supplement 1B-C), and (5) immunostaining of endogenous M2A (Figure 3—supplement 1D-F). Multiple independent approaches strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: M2A bipolar filaments assemble dynamically at the dSMAC:pSMAC boundary, move centripetally, expand into clusters through sequential amplification, and align with actin arcs to form the organized pSMAC actomyosin network. This process repeats continuously with new filaments appearing at the boundary.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 describe the dynamics of M2A assembly and organization. The time-lapse TIRF-SIM imaging (Figure 3B, Video 7) directly visualizes the sequential steps of filament appearance, centripetal movement, expansion, and alignment. The inference about sequential amplification (C68) is reasonable based on comparison to prior work in fibroblasts, though not directly demonstrated here.

results.result: ICAM-1 co-stimulation increases the synaptic content of M2A compared to anti-IgM stimulation alone, and this difference remains significant after normalizing for cell-spread area.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 show that ICAM-1 increases M2A recruitment. The quantification (Figure 3C-E, Figure 3—supplement 1G) demonstrates significantly higher M2A content with ICAM-1, and the normalization for cell area (Figure 3—supplement 1G) confirms this is not simply due to larger cell spreading. This supports the feed-forward mechanism proposed.

results.result: M2A contractility is required for the concentric organization of pSMAC actin arcs. Inhibiting myosin with pnBB disrupts arc organization, converting concentric arcs into disorganized mesh-like arrays, as quantified by anisotropy measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C73-C75 establish M2A's role in arc organization. The imaging (Figure 3F-G) clearly shows the transition from organized arcs to disorganized meshwork upon pnBB treatment, and the anisotropy quantification (Figure 3H) provides objective measurement of this disruption. This demonstrates that M2A contractility organizes the formin-generated filaments into arcs.

results.result: ICAM-1 co-stimulation increases traction forces, which are completely abrogated by myosin inhibition, indicating that integrin-dependent traction forces require M2A contractility. This likely reflects M2A pulling on LFA-1:ICAM-1 pairs and maintaining LFA-1 in its active conformation, suggesting a feed-forward relationship where integrin ligation promotes actomyosin arc formation and arc contractility promotes further integrin activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 link M2A contractility to traction forces and propose a feed-forward mechanism. The traction force microscopy data (Figure 3—supplement 2) clearly show ICAM-1-dependent force generation that is eliminated by pnBB. The proposed mechanism (C79, C81) is well-reasoned and supported by citations to prior work on integrin activation by mechanical force, though the feed-forward relationship is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network exhibits centripetal flow at ~1 μm/min in both primary B cells and A20 cells, approximately one-third the rate of dSMAC flow (~3 μm/min). This suggests that actomyosin arcs could contribute to inward transport of BCR:antigen clusters along with the dSMAC network.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 quantify actin flow rates in the pSMAC and dSMAC. The kymograph analysis (Figure 4—supplement 1) provides direct measurements showing consistent flow rates in both primary and A20 B cells. The inference that arcs could contribute to antigen transport (C86) is reasonable based on the centripetal flow, and is further tested in subsequent experiments.

results.result: The pSMAC actomyosin arc network works together with the dSMAC branched actin network to drive antigen centralization. Using PLBs, antigen microclusters were tracked moving inward at rates (2.36 μm/min in dSMAC, 1.03 μm/min in pSMAC) very similar to the rates of centripetal actin flow in each region.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C87-C91 demonstrate that antigen movement rates match actin flow rates. The tracking data (Figure 4B-C) shows antigen microcluster speeds that closely match the actin flow rates measured in Figure 4—supplement 1. The similarity in rates provides strong evidence that both actin networks contribute to antigen centralization, though the mechanism of coupling is addressed in subsequent claims.

results.result: Individual BCR:antigen microclusters are swept inward by individual actomyosin arcs via a sweeping mechanism likely dependent on frictional coupling. High-magnification TIRF-SIM imaging showed arcs moving antigen clusters, with pauses occurring when no arc was adjacent. The overall incidence of arc slippage must be small since antigen transport rate is not significantly slower than arc flow rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C92-C93 identify the mechanism of antigen transport by arcs. The high-magnification imaging (Figure 4D-G, Video 10) directly visualizes arcs sweeping antigen clusters, and the kymograph (Figure 4G) shows correlation between arc presence and cluster movement. The inference about frictional coupling is reasonable and supported by citations. The argument about low slippage incidence (C93) is logical based on the rate comparison.

results.result: The study recapitulated the integrin co-stimulatory effect using PLBs: B cells failed to centralize antigen at limiting density (0.15 μg/ml) without ICAM-1 but exhibited robust centralization with ICAM-1. At high antigen density (2 μg/ml), centralization occurred without ICAM-1. Multiple quantitative measures confirmed the co-stimulatory effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C103 establish the experimental conditions for testing myosin dependence. The imaging and quantification (Figure 5—supplement 1) clearly demonstrate the ICAM-1-dependent centralization at limiting antigen density using multiple metrics (distribution scoring, cSMAC content, cluster size vs. distance). This successfully recapitulates the Carrasco et al., 2004 findings and validates the PLB system.

results.result: Under integrin-dependent conditions (limiting antigen + ICAM-1), myosin inhibition with pnBB impairs synapse formation, as evidenced by failure to centralize antigen, absence of actin arcs, reduced antigen content at the synapse, and defective cSMAC formation. This demonstrates that the contractile actomyosin arc network plays a key role in integrin-dependent B-cell activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C104-C110 demonstrate the functional requirement for myosin in integrin-dependent IS formation. The imaging and quantification (Figure 5) show clear defects in antigen centralization, arc formation, and cSMAC formation upon pnBB treatment. Multiple quantitative measures (distribution scoring, cSMAC content, cluster size analysis) consistently show impaired IS formation. This is the key functional demonstration linking the actomyosin arcs to the integrin co-stimulatory effect.

results.result: Myosin inhibition under integrin-dependent conditions diminishes BCR signaling, as shown by reduced synaptic content of phosphorylated CD79a (P-CD79a) in pnBB-treated cells at both 5 and 10 minutes. This reduction is not due to differences in total CD79a content.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C111-C115 demonstrate impaired BCR signaling upon myosin inhibition. The imaging and quantification (Figure 6A-C, Figure 6—supplement 1A-B) show significant reduction in P-CD79a content in pnBB-treated cells at both time points, with appropriate controls showing no difference in total CD79a. This links the actomyosin arcs to BCR signaling.

results.result: Myosin inhibition causes defective signaling protein distribution at the synapse. P-CD19, normally enriched at the pSMAC/cSMAC boundary in control cells, becomes spread across the synaptic interface in pnBB-treated cells. pnBB treatment also reduces total synaptic P-CD19 content without affecting total CD19 content.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C116-C121 show disrupted distribution and reduced content of P-CD19 upon myosin inhibition. The imaging and line scans (Figure 6D-H) clearly demonstrate the altered distribution, and quantification (Figure 6F, Figure 6—supplement 1C) shows reduced P-CD19 without changes in total CD19. This further supports the role of actomyosin arcs in promoting BCR signaling.

results.result: The main conclusion is that integrin co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation and IS formation not only by enhancing adhesion but also by eliciting formation of a contractile actomyosin arc network that drives mechanical force-dependent IS formation. This contractile network plays a key role in the mechanism by which LFA-1 co-stimulation promotes B-cell activation when antigen is limiting.
results.evaluation: Claims C13 and C140 present the main conclusion integrating all findings. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective data showing: (1) ICAM-1 induces organized actomyosin arcs (C4, C34-C41), (2) arcs are created by mDia1 and organized by M2A (C5-C6, C42-C75), (3) arcs flow centripetally and sweep antigen (C7-C8, C82-C93), and (4) myosin inhibition impairs integrin-dependent IS formation and signaling (C9-C12, C104-C121). This represents a significant advance in understanding the mechanism of integrin co-stimulation.

results.result: About one-third of germinal center (GC) B cells exhibit robust actomyosin arcs in the pSMAC when engaged with anti-IgM/IgG and ICAM-1. These arcs co-localize with actin, move centripetally, and can surround centralized antigen, suggesting they may contribute to antigen centralization in GC B cells as well as naïve B cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C130 show that GC B cells can form actomyosin arcs. The imaging data (Figure 7A-D, Videos 11-12) demonstrate M2A enrichment in the pSMAC in ~1/3 of GC B cells, with arcs surrounding centralized antigen. However, the authors appropriately note that additional experiments are needed to fully characterize the role of arcs in GC B cells, including testing ICAM-1 dependence and quantifying contributions to traction forces and signaling.

results.result: GC B cells exhibit heterogeneous antigen distribution patterns: ~45% show peripheral clusters, ~20% show microclusters, and ~35% show centralized antigen. Cells with centralized antigen show pSMAC-like M2A accumulation, while cells with peripheral clusters or microclusters show less M2A and no organized pattern. The correlation suggests that GC B cells with centralized antigen are the ones making actomyosin arcs.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C138 characterize antigen distribution heterogeneity in GC B cells and correlate it with M2A accumulation. The imaging and quantification (Figure 7E-F, Figure 7—supplement 1) show the three distribution patterns and the correlation between centralized antigen and M2A accumulation. The inference that cells with centralized antigen make arcs (C137) is reasonable based on the ~1/3 frequency of both. However, the functional significance requires further investigation as noted by the authors.

results.result: The proposed mechanism linking integrin co-stimulation to actomyosin arc formation involves active RhoA, which would: (1) activate mDia1 at the plasma membrane, (2) activate ROCK-dependent phosphorylation of M2A regulatory light chains to promote M2A filament assembly, and (3) activate ROCK-dependent phosphorylation of mDia1's autoinhibitory domain to sustain its activity. Integrin ligation likely promotes RhoA activation through GEFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 propose a mechanistic pathway linking integrin ligation to arc formation through RhoA. While the proposed mechanism is well-reasoned and supported by citations to prior work on RhoA, formins, and myosin, it is not directly tested in this study. The pathway represents a logical hypothesis based on known signaling mechanisms, but experimental validation of RhoA activation, GEF involvement, and the specific phosphorylation events would be needed to confirm this mechanism.

results.result: The current findings differ from Bolger-Munro et al., 2019, who reported that BB treatment did not inhibit antigen centralization. The disparity may be due to differences in experimental design including cell type (primary vs. A20), antigen presentation mode (PLBs vs. APCs), and antigen density (known vs. variable).
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C150 address an apparent discrepancy with prior work. The authors appropriately acknowledge the difference and propose reasonable explanations based on experimental design differences. The most likely explanation is the use of limiting antigen conditions in the current study, which reveals the myosin dependence that may not be apparent under high antigen conditions. This highlights the importance of studying physiologically relevant conditions.

results.result: Prior studies of B-cell IS formation have primarily observed the dSMAC branched actin network in cells receiving antigen alone, almost exclusively in immortalized cell lines. Most in vitro studies have used excess antigen, while antigen is rarely available in excess in vivo, highlighting the importance of studying integrin co-stimulation under limiting antigen conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 and C141 provide important context about limitations of prior studies. These claims are supported by citations and highlight the novelty of the current work in studying primary B cells under limiting antigen conditions with integrin co-stimulation. This justifies the experimental approach and emphasizes the physiological relevance of the findings.
